courses.title: Weather Prediction Markets
courses.blurb: Ten lessons on what these contracts are, what settles them, and how to read a station’s day against the market pricing it.

lessons.title: How weather prediction markets work
lessons.aim: By the end, a viewer can read a price as a probability and knows why this exchange has no sellers.

parts.cue: Open on a city page with a live ladder beside the chart
text: A prediction market contract is a simple thing. It pays one dollar if a stated outcome occurs, and nothing if it does not. So the price of that contract, in cents, is what the market thinks the chance of that outcome is. A contract trading at thirty-six cents is a market saying there is roughly a thirty-six percent chance.

On this ladder each row is one outcome. The top one asks whether San Francisco’s high today will come in above seventy-eight degrees. Every row asks the same kind of question at a different temperature.

parts.cue: Zoom on one row, both coloured segments visible
text: Now the part that differs from a stock. On ForecastEx there are no sellers. Every order in the book is a bid to buy, and you can bid to buy Yes or bid to buy No. Those are the only two things anyone does. If you think the high clears seventy-eight, you bid to buy Yes. If you think it does not, you bid to buy No.

The two sides of a contract always sum to one dollar, because between them they cover everything that can happen. That is why the row is drawn as a single bar split into two. The green part is Yes and the red part is No, and together they are the whole dollar.

parts.cue: Hover the price to show the tooltip with both bids
text: The number printed on the row is the Yes price in cents. It sits midway between the best bid to buy Yes and one dollar less the best bid to buy No. Hover any price and you can see both of those bids for yourself. Where only one side has bids the number carries an asterisk, because half the information is missing and the midpoint is not really a midpoint.

parts.cue: Cut to a still diagram of a settled contract
text: When the day ends, every contract settles at either one dollar or zero. There is no partial credit. If you bought Yes at thirty-six cents and the outcome happens, you receive one dollar. If it does not, you receive nothing. Your risk was the thirty-six cents you put up, and it was known when you put it up.

One cost to keep in mind. The exchange charges one cent per contract to each side at execution. Nothing on this site is fee adjusted, so a price you see here is the exchange’s published price before that cent.

parts.cue: Back to the ladder, highlight one row
text: One last point, and it catches people. Buying Yes and buying No on the same contract is not a hedge and not a spread. The exchange nets them against each other, so the second purchase closes the first. If the two together cost more than a dollar, and after fees they usually do, you have simply locked in a loss. Positions across different strikes are a real thing and we cover them in the second course. Both sides of one strike is not.

quiz.q: A contract asking whether the high exceeds 78 degrees is priced at 36 cents. What is the market saying?
quiz.a: A roughly 36 percent chance the high exceeds 78.

quiz.q: On ForecastEx, what are the only two orders a participant can place?
quiz.a: A bid to buy Yes, or a bid to buy No.

quiz.q: You buy Yes and No on the same strike. What have you got?
quiz.a: Nothing. The exchange nets them, so the second trade closes the first, and the combined cost plus fees is a loss.

link.label: Open a city page and find a ladder

lessons.title: What settles a daily temperature contract
lessons.aim: By the end, a viewer can state exactly which number decides a contract and work out whether a given strike paid.

parts.cue: Open on the station location map on a city page
text: A daily temperature contract does not settle on the temperature in a city. It settles on the temperature at one specific weather station, and knowing which one is the whole game.

This is the map for San Francisco. The ringed station in the middle, labelled settlement station, is the one the contract resolves on. It is an airport weather station reporting on the hour, and its four-letter code is what the contract is written against. The other stations you can see are nearby fields reporting the same kind of data, and they are context. They settle nothing.

parts.cue: Cut to a still diagram of the settlement rule
text: Four things decide the outcome, in order.

First, the station. Second, the day, which is the local calendar day at that station, midnight to midnight in the station’s own time zone. A contract for the thirty-first is decided by what happens between local midnight and local midnight, not by a fixed window in a single time zone.
Third, the extreme over that day. For a high contract it is the highest temperature the station reported. That number is then rounded to a whole degree.

Fourth, the comparison, and this is where care pays. For a high, the contract pays if the rounded extreme is strictly above the strike. For a low, strictly below. Strictly means the strike itself does not count.

parts.cue: Worked example on the diagram, a day that lands on 79
text: Take the contract asking for a high above seventy-eight. The station reports seventy-eight point six. Rounded, that is seventy-nine. Seventy-nine is strictly above seventy-eight, so Yes pays.

Now the same contract with a day that reaches seventy-eight point four. Rounded, that is seventy-eight. Seventy-eight is not strictly above seventy-eight, so No pays. Two tenths of a degree separated those two days and they settled opposite ways. On days when the forecast sits near a strike, this is where the risk actually lives.

parts.cue: Scroll to the sources table on the FAQ page
text: One detail about the reports themselves. A station report carries the temperature twice, once in whole degrees in the body and once in tenths in the remarks. This site reads the tenths where they are available, and every observation snapshot records which convention produced it, so you can always see what a number came from. Special reports, the ones a station files between the hourly ones when conditions change, are counted too.

The FAQ page carries all of this in writing, along with every feed behind every page. If you take one thing from this lesson, take the strict inequality. It decides more contracts than any forecast does.

quiz.q: The station reports a maximum of 78.4 degrees. Does a contract asking for a high above 78 pay?
quiz.a: No. It rounds to 78, and 78 is not strictly above 78.

quiz.q: Which day bounds a daily temperature contract?
quiz.a: The local calendar day at the settlement station, in that station’s own time zone.

quiz.q: What role do the neighbouring stations on the map play in settlement?
quiz.a: None. They are context only.

link.label: Read the settlement convention in the FAQ

lessons.title: Reading the national board
lessons.aim: By the end, a viewer can scan every listed station at once and tell where the market and the forecast disagree.

parts.cue: Open on the landing map, Highs and today selected
text: This is every United States station the exchange lists, on one map. Each dot is a station, and what the dot encodes is a disagreement.

For each station the site takes the exchange’s ladder and finds the temperature where the Yes price crosses fifty cents, interpolating between the two strikes that bracket it. That is the market-implied median, the temperature the market is even money on. It then compares that against the National Weather Service forecast for the same day. The dot shows the difference.

parts.cue: Point at a warm dot, then a cool one
text: Warm colours mean the market is above the forecast. Cool colours mean it is below. The size of the dot is the size of the gap, so a big red dot is a station where the market is pricing a materially warmer day than the Weather Service is calling for.

parts.cue: Click through Lows, then the two Tomorrow buttons
text: Four buttons across the top. Highs and lows for the current day, and highs and lows for the day ahead. The day-ahead board is the one that lists first, so it is often where a new position goes on.

parts.cue: Hover a dot to open the tooltip
text: Hover any dot and the exchange’s own number comes first, because that is the thing being traded. Underneath it are the forecasts that inform it, for that side and that day only. The Weather Service forecast, the Blend of Models, the GFS statistical guidance, what the station has actually recorded so far today, and when its last report came in.

parts.cue: Hover a station whose board has not listed
text: Where a board has not opened yet there is no implied value to show, so the tooltip tells you when the contracts list and counts down to it. On a station where the ladder is listed but every strike sits far in or far out of the money, the ladder never crosses fifty cents and the site records no implied median rather than extrapolating past the strikes the exchange actually quoted.

parts.cue: Point at the pale shading behind the dots
text: The pale shading behind the map is an interpolation of the listed stations’ forecasts, drawn so you can see the shape of the day across the country. It is computed here, it is labelled derived, and it is not a National Weather Service product. Only the dots are contract data.

parts.cue: Click a dot to open its city page
text: Clicking any dot takes you to that station’s own page, which is where the next several lessons live.

quiz.q: What does a large warm dot indicate?
quiz.a: The market-implied median is well above the Weather Service forecast for that station and day.

quiz.q: How is the market-implied median found?
quiz.a: The temperature where the Yes price crosses 50 cents, interpolated between the two adjacent listed strikes.

quiz.q: Why might a listed station show no implied median?
quiz.a: Because the quoted ladder never crosses 50 cents, and the site will not extrapolate beyond the strikes the exchange quoted.

lessons.title: One station, hour by hour
lessons.aim: By the end, a viewer can read every line on the city chart and say what each one had seen when it was issued.

parts.cue: Open a city page chart, Today selected
text: This is one station, one contract day. The window runs from noon the day before through to the end of the contract day, so you can see the night that set up the morning.
The heavy white line is what the station has actually reported. Every dot on it is one hourly report. That line is the only thing on this chart that settles anything.

parts.cue: Point at each forecast line as it is named
text: Four forecast tools run underneath it, and each keeps the same colour everywhere on this site. Green is the National Weather Service, the official public forecast with a human forecaster’s judgment layered on. Orange dashed is the National Blend of Models, which is what those forecasters start from. Purple dotted is the aviation guidance, statistically corrected to this exact station and strong inside a day, though it only reaches about twenty-five hours. Grey is the GFS model output statistics, a single-model statistical product with no human editing.

parts.cue: Point at the dim dashed lines in the left half
text: The dim dashed lines are the same tools as they stood at six the evening before. That matters because a forecast issued this morning has already seen the overnight low, and one issued last night has not. Comparing them tells you how much a tool has changed its mind since the day began.

parts.cue: Point at the horizontal level lines and their labels
text: The horizontal lines are each tool’s forecast high and low for the day. The label carries the hour it was issued and whether that was today or the day before, so eleven p Y means eleven at night the previous day. That tag is there because when a forecast was issued decides how much of the day it had already seen.

parts.cue: Point at the vertical marks across the chart
text: The vertical marks are midnight, sunrise, sunset and the end of the day, plus when the exchange listed this board. The faint shading around the observed line is the five-minute data between hourly reports, which shows you a brief peak that fell between two reports. It is context and never settlement, and it is labelled that way.

parts.cue: Click Tomorrow, then Both days, then Overlay yesterday
text: Three buttons change the day. Tomorrow moves the whole chart to the day-ahead board. Both days shows them together. Overlay yesterday brings yesterday in at full strength with today stepping back, which is how you compare the shape of one day against the last.

parts.cue: Move the crosshair across the chart
text: Moving across the chart gives you a crosshair that reads every series at that instant, including the market price panels below. That is the fastest way to answer what everything thought at ten in the morning.

quiz.q: A level label reads 11p Y. What does that mean?
quiz.a: That forecast was issued at 11 at night on the day before the contract day.

quiz.q: Why is the aviation guidance line shorter than the others?
quiz.a: It reaches about 25 hours, so it ends where its horizon does.

quiz.q: Can the shaded band around the observed line settle a contract?
quiz.a: No. It is five-minute data shown for context; contracts settle on the hourly reports.

lessons.title: Strike ladders and Yes prices
lessons.aim: By the end, a viewer can read a whole board off the ladder and follow one strike through the day.

parts.cue: Open a city page, the ladder panel beside the chart
text: To the right of the chart is the whole board for this station and day. High strikes are stacked above, low strikes below, each one a row.

Every row is split green and red. Green is Yes and red is No, and the split is the price. A row that is nearly all green is a contract the market thinks will almost certainly pay. A row that is nearly all red is one it thinks will not.

parts.cue: Point at the numbers on the rows
text: The number on the row is the Yes price in cents, midway between the Yes bid and one dollar less the No bid. Where the number carries an asterisk, only one side has bids and the midpoint is standing on one leg. Rows outlined with a dotted border are the same warning drawn on the chart.

parts.cue: Hover a price, then click a strike
text: Hover any price to see the underlying bids and sizes. Click the price and it opens that contract on ForecastEx. Click the strike itself and it draws onto the temperature chart as a horizontal line, which is the quickest way to ask whether today’s observed line is anywhere near it.

parts.cue: Scroll to the two price panels below the chart
text: Below the chart are two price series, one for the high strikes and one for the lows. Each line is one strike’s Yes price sampled every ten minutes across two days. Watching a strike here against the observed temperature above it is the clearest picture of a market repricing as a day develops. A strike that starts the morning at fifty cents and is at eighty by noon is a market that has seen the heating run ahead of schedule.
parts.note: Language check for the narrator. Never say ask, sell or offer. There are only bids to buy Yes and bids to buy No. The feed’s ask on a Yes contract is one dollar less the No bid, and that is how the site computes the Yes price.

quiz.q: What does an asterisk beside a Yes price mean?
quiz.a: Only one side of that contract has bids, so the price is not a true midpoint.

quiz.q: How is the Yes price computed?
quiz.a: Midway between the Yes bid and one dollar less the No bid.

quiz.q: What does clicking a strike do?
quiz.a: Draws it on the temperature chart as a horizontal line.

link.label: Open a city page and its ladder

lessons.title: Variables upstream of temperature
lessons.aim: By the end, a viewer can judge whether a day is following the forecast’s physical story before the temperature confirms it.

parts.cue: Scroll to the additional variables panels
text: A temperature forecast is the end of a chain. Getting to a high of eighty-two takes particular ingredients, usually long unbroken sun, a certain amount of moisture in the air, and wind from a certain direction. If those ingredients are not showing up, the temperature will not either, and you can often see that before the thermometer does.

These panels show the chain directly. Temperature at the top, then sky cover, dewpoint, wind speed, and wind direction as barbs. Same tools, same colours, same window as the chart above, and the station’s own reports drawn on every one.

parts.cue: Point at the sky cover panel
text: Sky cover is the one to watch on a summer high. The tools that publish a percentage are drawn as that percentage. The tools that publish a category instead are drawn at the middle of the category, so few is nineteen percent, scattered forty-four, broken seventy-five and overcast a hundred. The Weather Service’s own wording maps onto the same scale. The observed line is the station’s reported cloud cover on that same scale.
If the forecast wanted clear skies through the late morning and the station is reporting broken cloud at ten, the day is not following the script and the high is likely to undershoot.

parts.cue: Point at the dewpoint and wind panels
text: Dewpoint is moisture, and a day that comes in more humid than forecast usually tops out lower. Wind speed reads in miles per hour. The barbs below give wind direction, using the standard convention where the staff points toward where the wind is coming from. A half barb is five knots, a full barb ten, and a pennant fifty. A wind that swings onshore ahead of schedule is a cooling story arriving early.

parts.cue: Point at the dim dashed lines
text: The dim dashed lines are the cycles that stood at six the evening before, carried across the whole window, so hours a morning update has not reached still show the forecast that stood for them.

parts.cue: Click Yesterday, the postmortem
text: The postmortem is where this becomes a habit worth having. It reads yesterday against the forecast that stood at six the evening before, which is the same moment the standings score. Beside it, the forecaster’s written discussion reverts to the one standing at that moment too. So you can ask what the tools said, what the sky actually did, and what the forecaster was thinking, all at the same instant, and find out which signal would have told you first.

quiz.q: A tool publishes broken cloud. What percentage is it drawn at, and why?
quiz.a: 75 percent, the midpoint of the broken band, so a categorical tool can share an axis with one that publishes percentages.

quiz.q: The staff of a wind barb points which way?
quiz.a: Toward the direction the wind is coming from.

quiz.q: What does the postmortem view hold fixed?
quiz.a: The forecast and the forecaster’s discussion as they stood at six the evening before the day being scored.

lessons.title: Live station observations
lessons.aim: By the end, a viewer can read an aviation station model and use neighbouring fields as an early signal.

parts.cue: Scroll to the station location map
text: This is the settlement station and every reporting field around it, each one carrying its current observation. The ringed station in the middle, labelled, is the one that settles. The others are context, and useful context.

parts.cue: Zoom on the key drawn in the corner of the map
text: Each station is drawn as a station model, which is a compact convention meteorologists have used for a century. Temperature sits at the upper left. Dewpoint at the lower left. The circle in the middle fills according to cloud cover, from empty for clear through to solid for overcast. And the line coming off it is a wind barb.

The barb points toward where the wind is coming from, so a barb pointing to the lower left means a wind out of the south-west. The marks on it are the speed in knots, a half barb for five, a full barb for ten, and a pennant for fifty. A small open circle instead of a staff means calm.

parts.cue: Hover the settlement station, then a neighbour
text: Hover any station for its full report with the time it was observed. The settlement station’s own reading is the one on the contract, and hovering it says so.

parts.cue: Point at a coastal station against an inland one
text: Here is why the neighbours matter. Weather arrives somewhere before it arrives everywhere. At a coastal station like this one, the marine air shows up at the fields nearest the water first, and the airport that settles the contract sees it half an hour or an hour later. Watching a temperature break at the coastal fields while the settlement station is still climbing is a genuine early signal, and it is visible here before it is visible in any forecast update.

parts.cue: Click Expand map
text: The map expands to fill the window when you want a closer look. The imagery is from the United States Geological Survey, which is why stations abroad show an outline rather than terrain.

quiz.q: On a station model, where is the dewpoint?
quiz.a: Lower left.

quiz.q: A barb has one pennant and two full barbs. What speed?
quiz.a: 70 knots.

quiz.q: Why watch a station that settles nothing?
quiz.a: Weather often reaches nearby fields first, so a neighbour can signal a change before the settlement station records it.

lessons.title: Forecaster reasoning and the station record
lessons.aim: By the end, a viewer knows where to read the forecaster’s own thinking and how to check a station’s recent history.

parts.cue: Point at the forecast discussion beside the panels
text: Every National Weather Service office writes an Area Forecast Discussion. It is a few hundred words from the forecaster on shift about what the models are doing, where they disagree, and what the office decided. It is the one place the reasoning behind a forecast is written down in plain language, and on a page showing a market disagreeing with a forecast it is the obvious next question.

It sits beside the variable panels, carried whole and unedited, with the office named, the issuance time given, and a link to the office’s own page. This site did not write it and does not summarise it. It is a United States government work in the public domain.

parts.cue: Scroll through a discussion, highlight a model-disagreement passage
text: What to look for is the passage where the forecaster names a split. When an office writes that the models diverge on timing, or that it went with one solution over another, you now know where the uncertainty is, and you can go and look at exactly that in the panels above.

parts.cue: Scroll to Last week at this station
text: Below, the station’s recent record. The first panel is each day of the past week, then the last three complete days broken out hour by hour on the same temperature scale, so a height means the same thing in both. This is where you learn a station’s habits. Some stations reliably run late to their high. Some hold a marine layer until eleven and then jump five degrees in an hour.

parts.cue: Scroll to Every scored day at this station
text: And the last table is every scored day at this station, each tool’s forecast beside what the station recorded. Every tool there was read at one moment, six in the evening the day before, so none of them had seen any of the day and every one had the same lead.

quiz.q: Who writes the Area Forecast Discussion?
quiz.a: The forecaster on shift at the National Weather Service office covering that area.

quiz.q: Is the discussion summarised on this site?
quiz.a: No. It is carried whole and unedited, with a link to the source.

quiz.q: At what moment is each tool read for the scored-day table?
quiz.a: Six in the evening the day before, so every tool has the same lead.

lessons.title: Scoring one day across the board
lessons.aim: By the end, a viewer can read one day across every station and spot a regional miss.

parts.cue: Open the scorecard page
text: The city page answers what happened at one station. This page answers what happened everywhere on one day.

Every station is a row. Each forecast tool is a column, and beside them is the temperature the station actually recorded. Errors are the forecast minus the observed, so a positive number means the tool ran warm.

parts.cue: Point at the sort order and the colour
text: Rows are sorted worst forecast first, because the interesting stations are the ones where something went wrong. Colour carries the size and direction of the error, so a band of red running down several neighbouring cities is a regional miss rather than a local one, and that is a different kind of information. A whole air mass arriving early will show up here as a row of stations missed the same way on the same day.

parts.cue: Switch the highs and lows toggle, then change the day
text: The toggle switches between the daily high and the daily low, and the day picker moves back through the scored days. Lows and highs fail differently, and a tool that is excellent on one is not automatically good on the other.

parts.cue: Hover a cell, then click a station
text: Hovering any cell gives the forecast, the observed value, the error, and which cycle that forecast came from with its lead to midnight. Clicking a station takes you to its own page for the same day.

quiz.q: A tool shows an error of plus three degrees. What does that mean?
quiz.a: The forecast was three degrees warmer than what the station recorded.

quiz.q: What does a band of similar errors across neighbouring cities suggest?
quiz.a: A regional miss, such as an air mass arriving earlier or later than forecast.

quiz.q: Why are rows sorted worst first?
quiz.a: The stations where the forecast failed are the informative ones.

lessons.title: Standings and what they mean
lessons.aim: By the end, a viewer can read the standings correctly and explain why the sample is matched.

parts.cue: Open the accuracy page, standings bars in view
text: Over the last two weeks of scored days, this is how far each tool has been from the temperature the station recorded, pooled across every station and ranked best first. The bar is the mean absolute error on the daily high.

Two things stand out. The first is how close they are. The whole field sits inside a fraction of a degree, which tells you these are all serious products and none of them is junk. The second is that the exchange’s own implied median is ranked here alongside the forecast systems, because the question the table answers is which of them has been closest, and that is arithmetic on published numbers.

parts.cue: Point at the caption below the bars
text: Now the part that makes the ranking honest. The sample is matched. Only station-days where every tool has a value are counted, so the number of days behind each bar is the same for all of them.

Without that, the table would be comparing tools over different days. The archives behind these lanes began on different dates, so pooling every error each tool happens to have would score one over three weeks and another over three days and then rank them against each other. Nothing would be wrong with any single number, but they would be answers to different questions.

parts.cue: Hover a bar to open its detail
text: Hover any bar for more than the headline. Bias tells you whether a tool runs warm or cold rather than just wrong, and a tool with a consistent bias is one you can correct for. The share within two degrees tells you about reliability rather than average error. And the same figures for the daily low are there, because a tool good at highs is not automatically good at lows.

parts.cue: Scroll up to the argument on the page
text: Above the standings, the page sets out why a market of participants with money at risk tends to land close to, and sometimes ahead of, the individual forecast systems it aggregates. Read that, then read the standings, and treat the ranking as evidence rather than as a claim.

quiz.q: What does a matched sample mean here?
quiz.a: Only station-days where every tool has a value are counted, so every tool is judged on the same days.

quiz.q: Why does that matter?
quiz.a: The archives began on different dates, so an unmatched pool would score different tools over different periods and rank them anyway.

quiz.q: What does bias tell you that mean absolute error does not?
quiz.a: Whether a tool runs consistently warm or cold, which can be corrected for.

courses.title: Trading Weather Markets
courses.blurb: Eight lessons on sizing a position across a ladder, the contract families beyond daily temperature, and one day worked from the evening before to settlement.

lessons.title: Sizing a position across a ladder
lessons.aim: By the end, a viewer can use the calculator to turn a forecast view into an allocation across strikes.

parts.cue: Open the position calculator, top figure in view
text: Everything so far has been about forming a view. This lesson is about turning a view into a position, and the thing that makes that non-obvious is the shape of the ladder itself.

For anything on a continuum, this exchange lists overlapping exceedance contracts. Take a hurricane wind ladder at one hundred and fifty, one hundred and forty, one hundred and thirty, one hundred and twenty and one hundred and ten miles an hour. These are not five separate bets. They all settle on the same wind.

parts.cue: Step through the three outcome rows of the figure
text: If the wind reaches one hundred miles an hour, every No pays and no Yes does. If it reaches one hundred and thirty-five, the Yeses on one thirty, one twenty and one ten pay, and the Nos on one forty and one fifty pay. If it reaches one hundred and fifty-five, every Yes pays.
So a position in one strike is a position in its neighbours, whether you meant it or not. Sizing strike by strike ignores that. The calculator does not.

parts.cue: Pick a live market from the picker
text: Start by choosing a market. It opens on a teaching example with made-up prices, and the picker loads any live ladder on this site, every daily temperature station, the hurricane counts, the climate series and the rest.

parts.cue: Enter a prediction and a span
text: Then you give it your view, in two numbers. The prediction is your median, the value you think the outcome is equally likely to land above or below. The span is your uncertainty, entered as a ninety-five percent interval, so it is the range you would be surprised to fall outside.

Those two numbers become a probability distribution. By default it is symmetric. For quantities whose misses are lopsided you can skew it either way, a long tail above for something like a wind speed or a rainfall total, a long tail below for something like a crop yield. Skewing keeps your prediction as the median and keeps the stated span as the ninety-five percent interval. What changes is how that span is divided between the two sides.

parts.cue: Point at the second column of the figure
text: Now the comparison. In the second column, the market’s Yes price for each strike is the green-to-red split. The arrow runs from that price to the value your own curve implies for the same strike. The length of the arrow is your disagreement with the market, strike by strike, and its direction tells you which side of that strike your view favours.

parts.cue: Enter a budget, point at the allocation and payout columns
text: Give it a budget and it allocates. The third column is where the money goes and the fourth is what the position pays back across the range of outcomes.

One constraint worth understanding. Allocation is confined to strikes the market prices between five and ninety-five percent. Outside that range the book thins out and a position sized against those prices could not reliably be filled. The payout multiples that make deep strikes look attractive are the least attainable numbers on the board. Those strikes stay drawn, faint, and take no capital.
parts.note: Say this on camera. The calculator never takes a view of its own. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type and the exchange’s published prices. The site adds no forecast and none of this is investment advice.

quiz.q: The wind reaches 135 mph on a ladder of 110 through 150. Which contracts pay?
quiz.a: Yes on 110, 120 and 130; No on 140 and 150.

quiz.q: What two numbers describe your view?
quiz.a: A median prediction and a 95 percent interval around it.

quiz.q: Why does allocation stop outside the 5 to 95 percent band?
quiz.a: The book thins there, so a position sized against those prices could not reliably be filled.

lessons.title: Risk aversion and the arithmetic
lessons.aim: By the end, a viewer can choose between the three allocation scenarios and knows what each one is optimising.

parts.cue: Open the calculator with a live ladder allocated
text: With a view and a budget fixed, one question is left. How aggressively to deploy the money. The calculator gives three answers and it is worth knowing what separates them.

parts.cue: Show the three scenarios in turn
text: The aggressive scenario concentrates capital in the few contracts your distribution says are most mispriced, the ones carrying the highest payout multiples, accepting that most of the capital may well be lost. The conservative scenario spreads capital broadly, accepting a lower best case in exchange for it being less likely that most of the capital goes. The middle scenario sits between them.

parts.cue: Cut to the allocation arithmetic section
text: The formal basis is the Kelly criterion. Each scenario chooses the allocation that maximises the expected utility of the payout under your own probability curve, computed jointly across the whole ladder rather than one strike at a time. That joint part is what respects the overlap we covered in the last lesson.

The middle scenario uses the logarithm as its utility, which is Kelly’s fully-invested form. At a single strike it splits money between Yes and No in your own probabilities, whatever the prices are. Across a ladder it tilts toward the strikes your curve prices furthest above their cost.

The conservative and aggressive scenarios use a more and a less risk-averse member of the same family of utility functions. Under the standard approximation those correspond to quarter-Kelly and double-Kelly risk appetites. The page cites Kelly’s original paper and the MacLean, Thorp and Ziemba treatment of the criterion’s good and bad properties, so you can go and read the basis rather than take it on trust.

parts.cue: Compare the payout column across two scenarios
text: What that means in the fourth column is visible. A more risk-averse utility is less tolerant of outcomes that pay nothing, so it buys the cheaper contracts on both flanks and produces a smoother payout curve. A less risk-averse one accepts the possibility of loss and concentrates near the centre of your prediction.

parts.cue: Set the prediction to match the market’s implied median
text: And a case worth sitting with. When your implied fair values and the market’s agree, no allocation split has an expected edge over another before the fee. The differences between the three scenarios are then purely about the smoothness of the payout. With the fee inside every scenario, an agreeing view is a reason not to trade rather than a choice about how.

quiz.q: What does the middle scenario maximise?
quiz.a: Expected log payout under your own probability curve, jointly across the ladder, which is Kelly’s fully-invested form.

quiz.q: Why is the allocation computed jointly rather than strike by strike?
quiz.a: The strikes overlap, so a position in one is a position in its neighbours.

quiz.q: Your view matches the market exactly. What does the calculator tell you?
quiz.a: No split has an expected edge before the fee, so the fee makes trading a losing proposition.

lessons.title: Tropical cyclone contracts
lessons.aim: By the end, a viewer can navigate the hurricane page and knows which record settles each kind of storm contract.

parts.cue: Open the hurricane page, active storms in view
text: Hurricane contracts come in three shapes. Counts over a season, landfall, and the winds of one storm while it is running. They settle on different records and they behave differently.

parts.cue: Point at a track, its cone, and the wind probability shading
text: At the top are the active storms, drawn from the National Hurricane Center. The line is the forecast track, the shaded region is the cone of uncertainty, which is where the centre is likely to go and not where the impacts are, and the wind-speed probabilities show the chance of a given wind arriving in a given place. Below them, the seven-day formation outlook, which is what the centre thinks may develop next. Alongside is the centre’s own written discussion for each storm, carried whole, the way the city pages carry the office discussions.

parts.cue: Scroll to season to date and count contracts
text: Then the count contracts. Atlantic named storms, hurricanes and major hurricanes, each with a ladder asking whether the season total exceeds a number.

What decides them is the season’s running count against the calendar. This panel draws the season to date against the climatological pace, which is where an average season sits on this date, and against the published seasonal forecast total. Both lines are drawn, so a forecast is never the only thing on the chart. The point of the pace line is that a count contract in early August is a very different proposition to the same contract in late October, because most of the season’s activity is still ahead in one case and behind in the other.

parts.cue: Scroll to the landfall panels
text: Landfall contracts ask whether a storm of a given strength makes landfall in a given place. They are low probability for most of a season and then move quickly, and the panels here show the record they settle against.

parts.cue: Scroll to the live-storm wind contracts
text: And the live-storm contracts, which are the fastest thing on this site. They ask about the wind at named reference locations, and the ladder updates delivery by delivery as the centre issues new advisories. This is where the exceedance ladder from lesson one is not an abstraction. A single advisory can move an entire ladder.

quiz.q: What does the cone of uncertainty show?
quiz.a: Where the storm’s centre is likely to track, not the extent of its impacts.

quiz.q: Why does the season panel draw the climatological pace?
quiz.a: The same count means different things at different points in the season, so the pace shows how much activity is still ahead.

quiz.q: What moves a live-storm wind ladder?
quiz.a: Each new advisory from the National Hurricane Center.

lessons.title: Severe weather, rain and drought
lessons.aim: By the end, a viewer can read a running month against its own history and knows which table settles a severe weather contract.

parts.cue: Open the weather page, tornado panel first
text: Severe weather contracts ask how many tornado, hail or wind reports the United States logs in a calendar month. They settle on the Storm Prediction Center’s monthly count, and the tornado reports lead this page because they are the family the exchange lists most actively.

parts.cue: Point at the running month figure
text: The running month is drawn the way the hurricane season is. The heavy line is this month so far. The faint lines behind it are the same month in past years, so you can see immediately whether this one is running hot or cold against its own history rather than against an abstraction.

A caution that matters here. A month that starts fast is not a month that ends high. Severe weather arrives in outbreaks, so a single active week can put a month ahead of pace and then three quiet weeks can bring it back. The historical lines show you how often that has happened.

parts.cue: Point at the ladder beside a listed family
text: Where the exchange lists a ladder for one of these, it is drawn beside the running count, so you can read the market against the pace directly. Where a family is not currently listed, the history is still here and the panel says it is not listed rather than hiding it.

parts.cue: Scroll through rain, monthly temperature, drought
text: The same page carries the other monthly quantities. Rain totals at Houston, Chicago, Miami, New York and Seattle. Monthly average temperature at Los Angeles, Chicago and New York. And United States drought coverage. Each is drawn as its published record with the listed strikes marked at the month each contract settles.

parts.cue: Point at a dashed continuation past the end of a record
text: One thing to read correctly. Past the end of each record a dashed line carries that calendar month’s usual value forward. That is a climatology. It is what the month normally does, and it carries no information whatsoever about the weather in this particular month. It is there to show where a strike sits relative to normal, not to forecast.

quiz.q: What record settles a US tornado count contract?
quiz.a: The Storm Prediction Center’s monthly count.

quiz.q: Why are past years drawn behind the running month?
quiz.a: So the current month can be judged against its own history rather than against an abstraction.

quiz.q: What is the dashed line past the end of a record?
quiz.a: A climatology, the month’s usual value, carrying no information about this month’s weather.

lessons.title: Climate contracts
lessons.aim: By the end, a viewer knows which long series the climate contracts settle on and how their publication schedules shape the trade.

parts.cue: Open the climate page
text: Climate contracts settle on long series that their publishers post on a fixed schedule. They are the slowest contracts on the exchange and the most different in character from a daily temperature.

parts.cue: Scroll through the series
text: The series carried here are global temperature, annually and monthly. United States temperature on the same two cadences. Atmospheric carbon dioxide. Global carbon dioxide emissions. Global sea level. And the strength of the Atlantic overturning circulation.
Each is drawn as its publisher posts it, with the listed strikes marked at the year each contract settles, so you can see the distance between where the series is and where the strikes are.

parts.cue: Drag across a chart to zoom
text: Drag across any chart to zoom into a period. On a series with decades of history that is how you read the recent behaviour against the long run.

parts.cue: Point at a strike marker near the current level
text: Two things make these contracts unlike a daily temperature. The first is publication schedule. An annual series resolves once a year on a date the publisher sets, and between those dates the contract moves on expectations rather than on data. Knowing when the next release lands is most of the calendar.

The second is that a year already largely elapsed carries a lot of information. A global temperature contract in November is being priced against a year that is ten months known and two months unknown, which is a very different proposition from the same contract in February.
parts.note: Handle with care on camera. These pages draw published records and listed strikes. Where a projection is drawn it is fitted from the record shown beside it and says so. The narration should not characterise where any of these series is heading.

quiz.q: What do the markers on a climate chart show?
quiz.a: The listed strikes, drawn at the year each contract settles.

quiz.q: Why does a global temperature contract behave differently in November than in February?
quiz.a: Most of the settlement year is already known by November, so far less of the outcome is still uncertain.

quiz.q: What moves these contracts between publication dates?
quiz.a: Expectations, since no new data on the settling series has been published.

lessons.title: Energy and agriculture contracts
lessons.aim: By the end, a viewer knows which agencies publish the settling numbers and why seasonality decides which strike is live.

parts.cue: Open the fossil fuels page
text: Energy contracts settle on series the Energy Information Administration publishes, and this branch of the site carries them all with the listed thresholds drawn on.

On the fossil fuel side, coal, natural gas and oil. Consumption in the United States and Canada, gas production, gasoline. On the electricity side, generation, price and revenue, across the fuels and renewables that produce it. Around thirty series in total.

parts.cue: Point at the seasonal shape of a consumption series
text: The thing to notice on almost every one of these is the seasonality. Natural gas consumption in January is a different animal from July. Electricity generation follows cooling demand. That shape matters because a threshold that looks impossibly far away in a shoulder month is routine in a peak one, and the strike a contract is written at only makes sense against the season it settles in.

The weather link is direct and it is why these contracts sit on this site at all. A cold January drives gas consumption. A hot July drives generation. The daily temperature markets and the energy markets are pricing related things.

parts.cue: Open the agriculture page
text: Agriculture is the smallest family here. World crop yields as the Department of Agriculture publishes them, corn, rice and wheat, with the listed thresholds marked. These resolve on scheduled agency reports, so like the climate contracts the release calendar is a large part of the trade.

quiz.q: Which agency publishes the series behind the energy contracts?
quiz.a: The Energy Information Administration.

quiz.q: Why does the season a contract settles in change how a threshold reads?
quiz.a: These series are strongly seasonal, so the same threshold is routine in a peak month and remote in a shoulder month.

quiz.q: What connects the energy contracts to the daily temperature ones?
quiz.a: Weather drives the demand these series measure, so they price related things.

lessons.title: Trading day, worked end to end
lessons.aim: By the end, a viewer has seen the whole workflow applied to one real day and can repeat it.

parts.cue: Recorded session, evening before, city page open
text: Everything in these two courses applied to one station and one day. It is the evening before, and the board for tomorrow has listed.

Start with the physical story. The Blend of Models is what the Weather Service forecasters start from, so read its forecast first and ask what has to happen for that number to verify. Suppose it calls for a high of eighty-two under mostly sunny skies with light south-west winds and a front passing after eight in the evening. That tells you the ingredients. Long unbroken sun and a late front. Note them, because those are the things you will check tomorrow.

parts.cue: Point at the ladder, then the implied median
text: Now the market. The ladder is pricing a median close to that eighty-two, which is what you would expect, since the market has read the same forecast. The question is not whether the market agrees with the forecast. It is whether the day is going to follow the script the forecast assumes.

parts.cue: Additional variables panels, evening before
text: Before leaving it for the night, check whether the tools agree on the ingredients rather than just on the number. Two tools can arrive at eighty-two by different routes, one with clear skies and a light wind, another with more cloud and a warmer air mass. When they disagree on the route, the temperature agreement is thinner than it looks and the day has more room to surprise.

parts.cue: Cut to next morning, live station map and panels
text: Morning. Now you are checking the script against reality, and the panels are ordered for exactly this. Sky cover first, because on a summer high it is the strongest lever. If the forecast wanted clear skies and the station is reporting broken cloud at ten in the morning, the heating is behind schedule. Dewpoint next. If the air is more humid than forecast, the high is likely to undershoot. Then the wind, where the direction is often more informative than the speed.

parts.cue: Station map, coastal fields against the airport
text: Then the station map, which is your earliest signal. If the fields upwind have already turned while the settlement station is still climbing, the change is on its way and you can see it before any forecast update carries it.

parts.cue: Back to the chart, observed line against the level lines
text: And the chart itself. By late morning the observed line has a shape. Compare it to where it needed to be for eighty-two, and to where the same station sat at the same hour on the days in the last-week panel that reached similar highs.

parts.cue: Open the calculator with this station’s live ladder
text: Say the evidence points one way. The sky cleared earlier than forecast, the dewpoint came in dry, and the station is running two degrees ahead of the days that finished at eighty-two. Now you have a view that differs from the board, and the calculator turns it into a position. Your median, your uncertainty, your budget, and an allocation that respects the overlap.

parts.cue: End on the settled day
text: Then the day settles, and the postmortem is not optional. Come back to the same page, switch the panels to yesterday, and look at what the tools had said at six the evening before, what the sky actually did, and what the forecaster had been thinking. Whether you were right or wrong, the question is which signal would have told you first. That is the habit that compounds.

quiz.q: Why start from the Blend of Models rather than the ladder?
quiz.a: It gives the physical story behind the forecast, which is what you then check the day against.

quiz.q: Two tools forecast the same high by different routes. What does that tell you?
quiz.a: The agreement is thinner than it looks, so the day has more room to surprise.

quiz.q: What is the point of the postmortem when you were right?
quiz.a: Finding which signal would have told you first, which is what makes the next day faster.

lessons.title: What this site does not do
lessons.aim: By the end, a viewer knows the site’s limits and what they must supply themselves.

parts.cue: Static frame, the site’s about page
text: Knowing where a tool stops is part of using it, so this last lesson is about the limits.

This site publishes no forecast of its own. It computes no fair value, no model probability and no measure of how wrong it thinks the market is. Every number on every page is either a published record from a government agency, a published price from the exchange, or arithmetic on numbers you typed in yourself. Where a projection appears it is fitted from the record beside it and says so.
That is a deliberate limit rather than a missing feature. What the site gives you is the same evidence the market has, laid out so you can read it faster. The view is yours to form.

parts.cue: Point at the freshness strip, then show it in a stale state
text: Second limit. Every page carries the time of the data it is drawing, not the time you loaded it. Observations and prices refresh every ten minutes and forecasts every thirty. If a feed falls behind, the page says so and keeps showing the last data it has rather than showing nothing. If a feed cannot be reached at all, the page shows the last copy your own browser saved, labelled as such. Check that strip before acting on anything.

parts.cue: Scroll the FAQ sources table
text: Third, provenance. The FAQ carries every feed behind every page, what it is, how often it is read, and what it settles. The weather content is United States government data. The handful of exceptions are named there individually rather than buried.

parts.cue: Closing frame
text: And the standing disclosure. This is not an Interactive Brokers or ForecastEx product, nothing on it is investment advice, and the prices it shows are the exchange’s published bids at the time stated, which can be stale. Trade on your own view, formed from evidence you have checked.

quiz.q: Does the site publish a fair value for any contract?
quiz.a: No. It publishes records, exchange prices, and arithmetic on numbers the user enters.

quiz.q: What does the freshness strip show?
quiz.a: The time of the data being drawn, not the time the page was loaded.

quiz.q: What happens when a feed cannot be reached at all?
quiz.a: The page shows the last copy the browser saved, labelled as such.
